idiom_name: one check-and-forward gate per boundary, composed into a chain, with identity carried as an explicit verifiable artifact
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give every gate the same request interface as the resource it protects; the gate resolves the caller's identity from evidence it can validate itself, evaluates its own policy, denies by default, and forwards to the next gate or handler only on success, recording every decision. Compose gates as wrappers around that interface (proxy objects, functions, middleware, filters or trait layers) so their order is configuration rather than code: the outermost gate sees the original request and the innermost sees the most constrained one. Carry identity as a verifiable artifact - a signed token, ticket, certificate chain or attribute set - and validate it at each boundary against an issuer both sides trust; never let an inner gate accept a claim merely because it arrived through the outer gate. What replaces the classic structure in practice: framework request pipelines (servlet filters, ASP.NET Core middleware, Rack-style middleware, tower layers, Ktor plugins) replace hand-written proxy chains and their registration; the classic form stays justified when the gates protect a non-HTTP interface or must be interposed below the framework.
code_sketch:
gate(policy, next):                       # one gate per trust boundary
    def handle(req, ctx):                 # ctx = identity verified so far
        actor, evidence = authenticate(req, ctx)     # own evidence, fail closed
        if not policy.allows(actor, req, evidence):
            audit.deny(actor, req); return Denied
        audit.allow(actor, req)
        return next(req, ctx.delegated(actor))

entry = gate(edge_policy, gate(inner_policy, resource))   # gates nest in order
pitfalls: An inner gate that accepts an identity the outer gate merely asserts (header, claim, source address) is not an independent gate: it rubber-stamps and creates a confused deputy.
Nesting the same check twice - same policy, same evidence - adds latency and operational surface without depth; independent layers must be able to fail independently.
Gate order carries meaning (bootstrap, credential extraction, audit, then authorisation); leaving it implicit in code instead of declaring it makes the effective policy depend on the environment.

Wrong move: pass the subject's credential through to the inner gate so it can authenticate for itself -> the outer gate now holds the subject's long-term secret and can impersonate it anywhere the secret works, and every rotation touches both ends -> instead forward a delegation or signed assertion scoped to the subject and transaction, which the inner gate verifies against a shared trust anchor.

Wrong move: treat the outer gate's identity header as proof of identity -> one unstripped or variably-canonicalised header (X-Forwarded-User vs X_Forwarded_User, a spoofed X-Forwarded-Uri) rewrites who the inner gate thinks is calling, as in the oauth2-proxy and Traefik header-smuggling advisories -> instead propagate mutual TLS or a signed assertion to the inner boundary and strip every client-supplied variant before authenticating.

Wrong move: let a gate error, timeout or JWKS fetch failure fall through to the handler -> an issuer outage or a revoked trust anchor silently converts the gate into a pass-through -> instead deny by default when evidence cannot be evaluated, cache trust material with bounded staleness, and alert on gate errors so fail-closed never becomes invisible downtime.
